ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The original study received ethical approval from [anonymized] (document: 043.2023).

Participants were recruited via a study link shared on social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Reddit, Instagram) and on mailing lists of people with misophonia who were willing to participate in misophonia research (e.g., the misophonia research pool from soQuiet).
Participants were incentivized through a lottery draw with a chance to win one of 48 vouchers worth $50 or £ 50.
A total of 734 participants were initially enrolled in the study, of whom 326 did not start the behavioral assessment or withdrew their data and were thus excluded.

We conducted post hoc data exclusions to remove participants who certainly did not have misophonia.foot_0 After data quality checks and exclusions (see supplemental materials), 370 participants were retained for the analysis.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were recruited via a study link shared on social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Reddit, Instagram) and on mailing lists of people with misophonia who were willing to participate in misophonia research (e.g., the misophonia research pool from soQuiet).

> Participants were incentivized through a lottery draw with a chance to win one of 48 vouchers worth $50 or £ 50.

> A total of 734 participants were initially enrolled in the study, of whom 326 did not start the behavioral assessment or withdrew their data and were thus excluded.

> We conducted post hoc data exclusions to remove participants who certainly did not have misophonia.foot_0 After data quality checks and exclusions (see supplemental materials), 370 participants were retained for the analysis.

> In line with the interpretation of classes, participants assigned to self-reported Class 2 (moderately elevated reactivity) and self-reported Class 4 (high reactivity) were more frequently classified into behavioral Class 1 (high reactivity).

Ethics approval statement:

> The original study received ethical approval from [anonymized] (document: 043.2023).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p < .05", "p < .05", "p < .05", 
"p > .05", "p < .05"), Text = c("Model-based composite reliability was low (ρ = .38) for reactive avoidance and high (ρ = .90) for anticipatory avoidance. 5 The unidimensional factor model for irritation reactions showed acceptable fit (χ²scaled(2) = 8.60, p < .05, robust CFI = .97, robust TLI = .90, robust RMSEA = .10, 90% CI [.03, .18], SRMR = .03) and composite reliability was moderate (ρ = .63).", 
"In contrast, the two avoidance behaviors were negatively correlated in the other two classes (r = -.28 in Class 2 and r = -.22 in Class 3, p < .05), whereas the associations involving sound aversion differed between the two classes.", 
"In the anticipatory-dominant reactivity class, reactive avoidance behavior was moderately and negatively associated with sound aversion (r = -.37, p < .05), whereas anticipatory avoidance behavior showed a positive but non-significant association with sound aversion (r = .20, p = .12).", 
"In contrast, although irritation and avoidance were moderately positively correlated in the total sample, the within-class correlations were weakly to moderately negative in the low and average reactivity classes (r = -.30 to -.49, p < .001) or negligible in the moderately elevated and high reactivity classes (-.01 to -.10, p > .05.", 
"Fisher's exact test indicated a small association between the behavioral profiles and the S-Five classification (p < .05; Cramér's V = .15)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .081", "p = .12", "p = .58", "p = .35", "p = .69", "p > .05", "p = .36"), Sentence = c("The bootstrap LRT comparing a three-to a four-class model was not significant (p = .081; #### Careless Responding

499 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **325 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  0 of 1 script ran without error when executed (1 more is run by another script with `source()`).
-  19 installable dependencies detected.
- 2 statistics stored from the extracted output; 0 of 14 reported tests matched (0%).

table.file_path: R-Scripts and Stan Models/Latent Profile Analysis.R

summary_table.ethics_statements: The original study received ethical approval from [anonymized] (document: 043.2023).
live_data_statements: Participants were recruited via a study link shared on social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Reddit, Instagram) and on mailing lists of people with misophonia who were willing to participate in misophonia research (e.g., the misophonia research pool from soQuiet).
Participants were incentivized through a lottery draw with a chance to win one of 48 vouchers worth $50 or £ 50.
A total of 734 participants were initially enrolled in the study, of whom 326 did not start the behavioral assessment or withdrew their data and were thus excluded.

We conducted post hoc data exclusions to remove participants who certainly did not have misophonia.foot_0 After data quality checks and exclusions (see supplemental materials), 370 participants were retained for the analysis.

In line with the interpretation of classes, participants assigned to self-reported Class 2 (moderately elevated reactivity) and self-reported Class 4 (high reactivity) were more frequently classified into behavioral Class 1 (high reactivity).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("1D OI-SB-IRT.R", "Latent Profile Analysis.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "1D OI-SB-IRT.R"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"dependency")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `final_data_val.rds` to `../Data/final_data_val.Rds` (in Latent Profile Analysis.R); `profile_data.Rds` to `../Data/profile_data.Rds` (in Latent Profile Analysis.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

**1 file name in the code is not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Latent Profile Analysis.R", "Name in the code" = "final_data_val.rds", 
    "Name in the deposit" = "final_data_val.Rds"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("1D OI-SB-IRT.R", "Latent Profile Analysis.R"
), Outcome = c("run_by_source", "timed_out"), Detail = c("", 
"timeout"), "Time (s)" = c(0, 300.3)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Latent Profile Analysis.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "C:/Users/Alina/Desktop/Promotion/3rd Article Misophonia Subgroup/Data Analysis"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Other changes we made to run the code**

Stan files in the syntax Stan removed in version 2.33 were given the newer syntax, and Git LFS pointers (placeholders a GitHub archive holds instead of the file) were replaced by the deposit's copy of the file. Updating the Stan files, and depositing the files themselves, solves this.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("R-Scripts and Stan Models/1D IRT model.stan", 
"R-Scripts and Stan Models/Hierarchical_IRT_model.stan", "1D OI-SB-IRT.R"
), Change = c("Stan from before 2.33: array declarations", "Stan from before 2.33: array declarations", 
"Stan in the R code, from before 2.33: array declarations")), row.names = c(NA, 
-3L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Run by another script**

1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "1D OI-SB-IRT.R", "Run by" = "Latent Profile Analysis.R"), row.names = "1D OI-SB-IRT.R", class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

info.title: Patterns of Reactivity in Misophonia: Profiles of Behavioral and Self-Reported Symptoms

author.affiliation:

text.text: Individuals with misophonia experience intense affective reactions to trigger sounds and often cope through avoidance.
Avoidance may be anticipatory (preventing exposure) or reactive (escaping exposure), but individual patterns remain poorly understood.
In a sample of individuals with misophonia (N = 370), we used Gaussian mixture modeling to identify profiles based on anticipatory avoidance, reactive escape, and emotional responses.
We compared profiles derived from behavioral assessments and self-reports and examined their associations with clinical outcomes.
Behavioral data revealed three qualitatively distinct profiles: high affective reactivity, anticipatory-dominant reactivity, and reactive-dominant reactivity.
Self-reports instead yielded four profiles that mainly reflected severity differences.
Agreement between methods was modest, suggesting that they capture partly different aspects of misophonic responding.
Behavioral profiles also differed in clinically relevant outcomes.
These findings highlight the value of behavioral assessment for identifying distinct response styles and advancing understanding of misophonia beyond symptom severity.
Misophonia is conceptualized as a sound sensitivity disorder involving emotionally distressing reactions to specific sounds, referred to as "triggers" (see Swedo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Misophonia is conceptualized as a sound sensitivity disorder involving emotionally distressing reactions to specific sounds, referred to as "triggers" (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Swedo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These emotional and physiological reactions range from irritation, heightened arousal, and physical pain to intense panic and rage (e.g., Rosenthal et al., 2022; Rouw & Erfanian, 2018), which can cause significant distress and interference with social and daily functioning (Jager et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These emotional and physiological reactions range from irritation, heightened arousal, and physical pain to intense panic and rage (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Rosenthal et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Rouw & Erfanian, 2018)</ref>, which can cause significant distress and interference with social and daily functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Jager et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with misophonia typically engage in some form of avoidance behavior when confronted with (potential) situations with trigger sounds (e.g., Cowan et al., 2022; Ozuer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Individuals with misophonia typically engage in some form of avoidance behavior when confronted with (potential) situations with trigger sounds (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Cowan et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Ozuer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, the current consensus definition indicates avoidance as the most prevalent behavioral response within the phenomenology of misophonia and an important consideration in emerging diagnostic frameworks (Swedo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, the current consensus definition indicates avoidance as the most prevalent behavioral response within the phenomenology of misophonia and an important consideration in emerging diagnostic frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Swedo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, the ways in which individuals respond to trigger sounds are not uniform, and avoidance may manifest in overt and more subtle forms.

For example, while some individuals endure aversive sounds with heightened emotional arousal, others avoid or escape such situations with triggers to prevent potential exposure or reduce emotional burden (e.g., Jager et al., 2020).
text.formatted: For example, while some individuals endure aversive sounds with heightened emotional arousal, others avoid or escape such situations with triggers to prevent potential exposure or reduce emotional burden (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Jager et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This illustrates at least two functionally distinct behavioral reactions: 1) anticipatory avoidance, referring to the prevention of trigger exposure, and 2) reactive avoidance, referring to escape during exposure.
Although both forms serve to reduce aversive states, they differ in timing, underlying learning mechanisms, and regulatory competencies and demands.
Despite this variability in the presentation of misophonia, categorical frameworks tend to collapse different constellations of these symptoms under the diagnostic label of misophonia.
Shifting the emphasis from a purely categorical approach toward a more dimensional and functional understanding of psychopathology has been advocated for decades (Insel et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Shifting the emphasis from a purely categorical approach toward a more dimensional and functional understanding of psychopathology has been advocated for decades <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Insel et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, Remmert, Schmidt, et al. (2022) and Woolley et al. (2025) argue for a symptom-oriented, dimensional perspective on misophonia to account for its phenomenological complexity and, consequently, yield a more differentiated understanding of interindividual variability in misophonia.
text.formatted: Thus, <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Remmert, Schmidt, et al. (2022)</ref> and <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al. (2025)</ref> argue for a symptom-oriented, dimensional perspective on misophonia to account for its phenomenological complexity and, consequently, yield a more differentiated understanding of interindividual variability in misophonia.

text.text: Previous studies have already aimed to account for this variability in misophonia by identifying latent subgroups (Andermane et al., 2023; McKay et al., 2018; Norris et al., 2022 Norris et al., , 2024;; Woolley et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Previous studies have already aimed to account for this variability in misophonia by identifying latent subgroups <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andermane et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">McKay et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Norris et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Norris et al., , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite methodological differences, studies most consistently identified severity-based subgroups that distinguished individuals with low, moderate, and high levels of misophonic symptoms, indicating only quantitative, not qualitative, distinctions.
Approaches combining misophonic symptoms with broader sensory processing and psychiatric symptoms have identified more differentiated patterns.

For example, Norris et al. (2022) found three distinct symptom profiles: 1) a relatively unaffected group, 2) a "pure" sensory group with severe misophonia symptoms but few psychiatric comorbidities, and 3) a broad sensory and psychiatric group.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Norris et al. (2022)</ref> found three distinct symptom profiles: 1) a relatively unaffected group, 2) a "pure" sensory group with severe misophonia symptoms but few psychiatric comorbidities, and 3) a broad sensory and psychiatric group.

text.text: The most recent study by Woolley et al. (2025) used indicators from a standardized clinical interview of misophonic symptoms and identified two subgroups based on the temporal dynamics of responses to triggers labeled "anticipatory" and "reactive."
text.formatted: The most recent study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al. (2025)</ref> used indicators from a standardized clinical interview of misophonic symptoms and identified two subgroups based on the temporal dynamics of responses to triggers labeled "anticipatory" and "reactive."

text.text: The anticipatory group showed higher awareness of potential triggers and higher levels of negative emotions and rumination prior to sounds than the reactive group.
These findings also show qualitative differences in how misophonia is experienced and expressed.

Previous attempts to identify subgroups have primarily used broad symptom constellations as indicators of subgroups, which may conflate symptom severity with the specific regulatory mechanisms and temporal dynamics of reactions to trigger sounds.

For example, some individuals may primarily react to reduce immediate sensory distress elicited by trigger sounds, whereas others may engage in anticipatory behavior to prevent expected aversive outcomes associated with potential triggers.
This distinction may also reflect different mechanisms in the development or maintenance of misophonia that have not yet been investigated.

As a result, it remains unclear whether previously identified subtypes reflect differences in overall symptom severity or rather qualitatively distinct reactive profiles of responding to trigger sounds.
Previous subgroup investigations have relied almost exclusively on dispositional selfreport measures.
However, avoidance and reactivity processes unfold dynamically within specific contexts and may not be fully captured through retrospective reporting (see Remmert, Oh, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, avoidance and reactivity processes unfold dynamically within specific contexts and may not be fully captured through retrospective reporting (see <ref type="bibr">Remmert, Oh, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, direct behavioral assessment allows for examining how individuals respond to trigger exposure in contextualized, controlled settings and to test whether dispositional tendencies align with situational behavior.
Consequently, results from subgroup analyses may differ when based on dispositional self-reports rather than situational behavioral measures.

While we have found that measures of different forms of avoidance differ between dispositional self-reports and situational behavioral measures (see Remmert, Gregory, et al., 2026), we do not know how this affects subgroup analyses.
text.formatted: While we have found that measures of different forms of avoidance differ between dispositional self-reports and situational behavioral measures (see <ref type="bibr">Remmert, Gregory, et al., 2026)</ref>, we do not know how this affects subgroup analyses.

text.text: Building on Woolley et al. (2025), we aim to identify and investigate subgroups explicitly based on indicators of affective reactivity.
text.formatted: Building on <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al. (2025)</ref>, we aim to identify and investigate subgroups explicitly based on indicators of affective reactivity.

text.text: By reactivity, we refer to affective and behavioral responses elicited by trigger stimuli.
This includes aversive emotional responses and attempts to escape or prevent stimulus exposure.
We propose that misophonia may be characterized not merely by differences in symptom intensity, but by distinct mechanisms of anticipatory avoidance, reactive escape, and emotional reactions.
Importantly, different reactivity styles may not be equally associated with functional impairment.

For instance, persistent anticipatory avoidance may lead to cumulative social restriction and environmental narrowing, whereas predominantly reactive responding may be associated with situational distress but with less pervasive interference in daily life.

Thus, identifying subgroups with qualitatively different reactivity behavior may help explain why individuals with comparable levels of misophonic distress differ in the degree of impairment they experience.
Different from previous studies, we consider both dispositional self-report data and situational behavioral measures and compare the results.

Specifically, we a) identify subgroups based on behavioral indicators of anticipatory and reactive avoidance during direct exposure, b) identify subgroups based on dispositional indicators of anticipatory avoidance, reactive avoidance, and emotional reactions, c) examine the correspondence between dispositional and behavioral subgroup solutions, and d) explore whether identified reactivity styles differ in misophonia-related and other clinical variables.

By considering patterns of reactivity processes rather than symptom severity, this approach aims to clarify whether distinct reactivity styles are differentially associated with clinical functional outcomes.
The present study relies on existing data collected during the development of the Misophonic Behavioral Avoidance Test (M-BAT; Remmert, Gregory, et al., 2026) and was partly preregistered.
text.formatted: The present study relies on existing data collected during the development of the Misophonic Behavioral Avoidance Test (M-BAT; <ref type="bibr">Remmert, Gregory, et al., 2026)</ref> and was partly preregistered.

text.text: Supplemental materials, the underlying data, the preregistration, and the code used in the analyses are openly accessible at: https://osf.io/p2xhe/overview?view_only=9556ac5ed57c4b18a27bbf3070638640.
text.formatted: Supplemental materials, the underlying data, the preregistration, and the code used in the analyses are openly accessible at: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/p2xhe/overview?view_only=9556ac5ed57c4b18a27bbf3070638640">https://osf.io/p2xhe/overview?view_only=9556ac5ed57c4b18a27bbf3070638640</ref>.

text.text: The original study received ethical approval from [anonymized] (document: 043.2023).

Participants were recruited via a study link shared on social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Reddit, Instagram) and on mailing lists of people with misophonia who were willing to participate in misophonia research (e.g., the misophonia research pool from soQuiet).

Individuals who accessed the study link were directed to the platform (Tivian XI GmbH, 2024) to view an online information page and provide informed consent before completing eligibility screening and the first part of the survey.
text.formatted: Individuals who accessed the study link were directed to the platform <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Tivian XI GmbH, 2024)</ref> to view an online information page and provide informed consent before completing eligibility screening and the first part of the survey.

text.text: Eligible participants then completed an online behavioral avoidance assessment via Pavlovia (Pavlovia Team, 2024), followed by a second survey in Unipark.
All assessments were completed remotely by participants using their own computers in their chosen environment.
Participants were incentivized through a lottery draw with a chance to win one of 48 vouchers worth $50 or £ 50.

Inclusion criteria of the original study were a positive one-item screening for misophonia (see measures section for details), age above 18 years, no hearing loss, disability, or epilepsy, a quiet test environment, access via computer with keyboard, and at least intermediate English proficiency.
A total of 734 participants were initially enrolled in the study, of whom 326 did not start the behavioral assessment or withdrew their data and were thus excluded.

We conducted post hoc data exclusions to remove participants who certainly did not have misophonia.foot_0 After data quality checks and exclusions (see supplemental materials), 370 participants were retained for the analysis.
text.formatted: We conducted post hoc data exclusions to remove participants who certainly did not have misophonia.<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> After data quality checks and exclusions (see supplemental materials), 370 participants were retained for the analysis.

text.text: The sample is primarily female (75.4%) and White (85.8%), has a high level of education, and has an average age of 39.3 years (SD = 14.0); see Table S1 in the supplemental material for details on sociodemographic characteristics.
text.formatted: The sample is primarily female (75.4%) and White (85.8%), has a high level of education, and has an average age of 39.3 years (SD = 14.0); see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> in the supplemental material for details on sociodemographic characteristics.

text.text: All individuals reported symptoms of misophonia, with most participants having clinically significant symptoms according to different classifications.
More than half of the sample reported suffering from a mental disorder (50.1 %), with 34.3 % currently receiving treatment; see Table 1 for clinical characteristics.
text.formatted: More than half of the sample reported suffering from a mental disorder (50.1 %), with 34.3 % currently receiving treatment; see Table <ref type="table">1</ref> for clinical characteristics.

The category 'subclinical' describes individuals who fulfilled all criteria but did not exhibit functional impairment/distress.
'Impaired' describes individuals who fulfilled the criterion of functional impairment/distress and at least one other criterion but not all.

The DVMSQ is a screening questionnaire for misophonia with 21 items: a single binary screening question, 12 'symptom frequency' items rated on a 5-point rating scale (0 = 'never' to10 = 'very often'), and 8 'impairment' items rated on a 5-point rating scale (0 = 'not at all' to10 = 'an extreme amount').
Empirical evidence showed excellent reliability (.93 ≤ ωT ≤ .98) and first evidence of validity (Williams et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence showed excellent reliability (.93 ≤ ωT ≤ .98) and first evidence of validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Williams et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The DMQ is a process-based questionnaire assessing facets of misophonia.
Sixteen items from the subscales coping strategies before and coping strategies during being triggered were administered.
The items are rated on a 5-point rating scale (0 = 'never' to4 = 'always/almost always'), with higher scores reflecting more frequent behavior over the past month.
The administered subscales have demonstrated good reliability, a well-established latent structure, and evidence of validity (Rosenthal et al., 2021; Shan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The administered subscales have demonstrated good reliability, a well-established latent structure, and evidence of validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Rosenthal et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The DMQ is used as an outcome measure.
The S-Five-E is a section of the S-Five, comprising 25 items across five subscales: internalizing appraisals, externalizing appraisals, perceived emotional threat, outbursts, and impact.
Items are rated on an 11-point rating scale (0 = 'not at all true' to10 = 'completely true'), with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.

Several studies replicated high reliability, latent structure, and evidence of validity (Remmert, Jebens, et al., 2022; Uglik-Marucha et al., 2024; Vitoratou et al., 2021 Vitoratou et al., , 2022 Vitoratou et al., , 2023;; Wang et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Several studies replicated high reliability, latent structure, and evidence of validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Remmert, Jebens, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Uglik-Marucha et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Vitoratou et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Vitoratou et al., , 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Vitoratou et al., , 2023;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Wang et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The S-Five-E is used as an outcome measure.
The BMQ-R is a modular, symptom-oriented questionnaire that measures misophonic symptoms.

Sixty-four items from eighteen subscales were administered: physical, anger, irritation, disgust, anxiety reactions to both the presence and anticipation of sounds, as well as general, behavioral, cognitive, and emotional dysregulation, reactive and anticipatory avoidance behavior, distress, and functional impairment.
Items are rated on a 6-point rating scale (0 = 'strongly disagree' to5 = 'strongly agree'), with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.
Participants rated the items with reference to the sounds that most bother and stress them.

Empirical evidence supports reliability (.72 ≤ ω ≤ .94), the factorial structure, and validity within a nomological network (Krog et al., 2024; Remmert, Jebens, et al., 2022; Remmert, Schmidt, et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Empirical evidence supports reliability (.72 ≤ ω ≤ .94), the factorial structure, and validity within a nomological network <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Krog et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Remmert, Jebens, et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Remmert, Schmidt, et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The subscales irritation reactions to the presence of sounds, reactive avoidance, and anticipatory avoidance were used as indicators of the latent profiles for self-reported dispositional affective reactivity.
All other subscales were used as clinical outcome measures.
The M-BAT is a standardized behavioral assessment designed to measure both reactive and anticipatory avoidance tendencies in response to misophonic auditory stimuli.
The procedure comprises two subtests that differ in the type of exposure.
Sound endurance (i.e., reactive avoidance behavior) is measured through unannounced exposure to a series of 18 stimuli.
For each stimulus, respondents are instructed to endure the sound for up to 15 seconds but may terminate the exposure at any time if it becomes intolerable, yielding endurance times.
Anticipatory avoidance tendency and speed are measured by announced exposure to a separate, comparable series of 18 stimuli.

Each upcoming stimulus is announced via a textual description, after which respondents decide whether to engage with the stimulus (5 s exposure) or omit the exposure altogether, yielding omission indicators and corresponding omission response times.

Anticipatory avoidance tendency reflects the tendency to omit exposure to stimuli, and anticipatory avoidance speed is the speed at which individuals decide to omit such exposure (with higher values indicating faster, more automatic responses).
In addition, subjective sound aversion is measured for presented stimuli using a 7-point unipolar rating scale (1 = 'not unpleasant' to7 = 'extremely unpleasant').
Additionally, the number of triggers per individual was defined as the number of stimuli receiving a rating of 6 or higher.

Stimuli were selected from established misophonia stimulus databases (Misophonia Audiovisual Trigger Archive; Oh et al., 2026; Free Open-Access Misophonia Stimuli Database; Orloff et al., 2023) to represent major classes of misophonic triggers.
text.formatted: Stimuli were selected from established misophonia stimulus databases (Misophonia Audiovisual Trigger Archive; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Oh et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Free Open-Access Misophonia Stimuli Database;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Orloff et al., 2023)</ref> to represent major classes of misophonic triggers.

text.text: Specifically, the test consists of six eating sounds, six breathing/throat sounds, and six environmental sounds.
All stimuli were standardized for duration and loudness.
Reactive avoidance, anticipatory avoidance tendency, and sound aversion are used as indicators of latent profiles for situational behavioral reactivity.
Anticipatory avoidance speed and the number of triggers are used as clinical outcome measures.

Individuals were asked to indicate how often, on a typical day, they prevent exposure to trigger sounds related to eating, breathing/throat sounds, and environmental sounds, and how often they escape from their vicinity.
The questions were specifically developed for this study and used as an outcome measure.
All analyses were conducted using R (R Core Team, 2026; version 4.6.1) and Stan (Stan Development Team, 2026).
text.formatted: All analyses were conducted using R (R Core Team, 2026; version 4.6.1) and Stan <ref type="bibr">(Stan Development Team, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Irritation reactions to the presence of sounds are modeled using a unidimensional factor model.
Reactive and anticipatory avoidance were modeled using a twodimensional correlated factor model.
All confirmatory factor models were estimated using robust Full Information Maximum Likelihood estimation (MLR and FIML) and identified via latent variable standardization.
2 M-BAT Measures.
Sound endurance is modeled using a unidimensional One-Inflated SB-IRT model (see Remmert, Oh, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Sound endurance is modeled using a unidimensional One-Inflated SB-IRT model (see <ref type="bibr">Remmert, Oh, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The model is estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling with two chains, each with 30,000 iterations and half burnin.
For identification, we standardized latent sound endurance 3 .
Anticipatory avoidance tendency is modeled with a 2-PL IRT model for sound omission indicators.
The model is estimated using MCMC sampling with two chains, each with 15,000 iterations and half burnin.
For identification, we standardized the latent anticipatory avoidance tendency.

Anticipatory avoidance speed is modeled using a generalized log-normal measurement model (Remmert, Oh, et al., 2026) for omission times, and a two-dimensional hierarchical model that combines the two measurement models of anticipatory avoidance tendency and speed 4 .
text.formatted: Anticipatory avoidance speed is modeled using a generalized log-normal measurement model <ref type="bibr">(Remmert, Oh, et al., 2026)</ref> for omission times, and a two-dimensional hierarchical model that combines the two measurement models of anticipatory avoidance tendency and speed 4 .

text.text: For sound aversion, we defined a formative operationalization using an equally weighted mean score index of person parameter estimates from unidimensional models of unpleasantness ratings for a) eating sounds, b) breathing/throat sounds, and c) environmental sounds.
For more details, see the supplemental materials.

2 Although the indicators were ordinal, MLR estimation was used because the items had six response categories, for which treating them as continuous is generally appropriate (e.g., Rhemtulla et al., 2012).
text.formatted: 2 Although the indicators were ordinal, MLR estimation was used because the items had six response categories, for which treating them as continuous is generally appropriate (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Rhemtulla et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: 3 Because sound endurance reflects the negative pole of reactive avoidance, person parameter estimates were reversed to directly reflect reactive avoidance and facilitate interpretability.
4 Stimulus omission times are missing by design when a stimulus was not omitted.
The missingness mechanism was addressed using a joint modeling approach, following the assumptions described in Remmert, Oh, et al. (2026).
text.formatted: The missingness mechanism was addressed using a joint modeling approach, following the assumptions described in <ref type="bibr">Remmert, Oh, et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: See the supplemental materials for details.
Outcome Measures.

Misophonic symptoms used as outcome measures were modeled according to the measurement models proposed by the original authors using confirmatory factor analysis with robust full-information maximum likelihood estimation and latent variable standardization for model identification.
Details are provided in the supplemental materials.
We specified Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to uncover latent groups for each measurement method.
For situational behavioral reactivity, we used Expected A Posteriori (EAP) estimates of reactive avoidance, anticipatory avoidance tendency, and formative scores of sound aversion.

For self-reported dispositional reactivity, we estimated factor scores using Empirical Bayes Modal (EBM) estimates from the respective measurement models of irritation reactions, reactive avoidance, and anticipatory avoidance.
Irritation reactions were selected as the most comparable self-report indicator to unpleasantness ratings (i.e., sound aversion).
All profile indicators were z-standardized for the latent profile analyses.
GMM assumes that the data arise from a mixture of several latent normally distributed populations, i.e., distinct subgroups.

They also make assumptions about the covariance structure within and between these groups, i.e., whether volume (overall variability), shape (relative variability of indicators), and orientation (correlations between indicators) are constrained to be equal or allowed to vary across groups.
As no strong assumptions could be made regarding the model parameters, we specified models with varying constraints to evaluate them empirically.

Model fit was evaluated using Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and Integrated Complete-data Likelihood (ICL) as provided in the mclust package (Scrucca et al., 2023), with higher values indicating better model fit.
text.formatted: Model fit was evaluated using Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and Integrated Complete-data Likelihood (ICL) as provided in the mclust package <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Scrucca et al., 2023)</ref>, with higher values indicating better model fit.

text.text: To determine the number of groups, bootstrap likelihood ratio tests (LRTs), entropy, class separation plots, average posterior class probabilities, and theoretical interpretability were used for model selection.
The latent groups identified by the profile analyses were compared on relevant clinical variables using Welch's analysis of variance (Welch ANOVA) followed by Games-Howell post hoc tests.

text.text: Most notably, two classes exhibited pronounced discrepancies in anticipatory avoidance: one class showed elevated behavioral but comparatively reduced self-reported anticipatory avoidance, whereas the other showed the opposite pattern.
These findings suggest that behavioral and self-reported measures may capture partially distinct aspects of affective reactivity.
The primary objective of this study was to investigate whether individuals with misophonia exhibit qualitatively distinct patterns of affective reactivity.
We found substantially different results when evaluating this question using dispositional self-report measures versus situational behavioral measures.

For the behavioral measures, we found qualitatively distinct behavioral profiles: 1) high affective reactivity, characterized by high levels of reactive avoidance, anticipatory avoidance, and subjective sound aversion; 2) anticipatory-dominant reactivity, exhibiting average levels of anticipatory avoidance, low reactive avoidance, and low sound aversion; and 3) reactive-dominant reactivity, characterized by above-average reactive avoidance and sound aversion, and low anticipatory avoidance.
While individuals with high aversion exhibit both types of avoidance behavior, individuals with somewhat lower aversion tend to exhibit only one.
Importantly, the profiles identified through standard self-report questionnaires showed only quantitative differences, not qualitative ones.
One explanation for this discrepancy may lie in the type of information captured by the two assessment modalities.
Behavioral assessment captures responses in standardized situations and is therefore better suited to capture the temporal and functional dynamics of avoidance behavior.

In contrast, retrospective self-report measures necessarily aggregate experiences across multiple situations and time periods without a specific frame of reference, potentially averaging over distinct response tendencies into more global evaluations of symptom burden.

Furthermore, the behavioral measure assesses reactions to specific trigger sounds that are the same for all individuals, whereas self-reports do not specify any particular sounds; each participant may refer to different sounds and situations.
At the same time, self-reports may be confounded by specific response biases, such as limited introspection and recall biases, whereas behavioral measures are less susceptible to these influences.

Thus, the behavioral measure provides a more direct and standardized assessment of behavior, thereby facilitating comparison across individuals, whereas self-reports may better capture individuals' perceived behavior across everyday contexts.

Individuals with contradictory measures on self-reports and behavioral measures may, thus, be those a) for which the sounds in the behavioral measure do not represent triggers, b) that show response bias in the self-reports, c) that behave differently in testing situations than in real life, and/or d) whose subjective appraisal of their reactions differs from their observable behavior.

Although the identified profiles differed structurally depending on the assessment modality (self-report vs. behavioral), both high affective reactivity profiles consistently aligned with the most severe self-reported misophonia symptoms, including the greatest functional impairment.
This pattern might suggest that greater avoidance, whether reactive or anticipatory, simply reflects greater emotional reactivity and overall symptom severity.

However, the anticipatory-dominant behavioral profile challenges this linear assumption, with individuals in the group showing the lowest overall misophonia symptoms when behavioral groups were compared on misophonia severity self-report scales and on overall reactivity.

In contrast to Woolley et al. (2025), who found greater symptom severity in the anticipatory subgroup, the present findings suggest that a tendency toward anticipatory avoidance may emerge independently of overall symptom severity.
text.formatted: In contrast to <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al. (2025)</ref>, who found greater symptom severity in the anticipatory subgroup, the present findings suggest that a tendency toward anticipatory avoidance may emerge independently of overall symptom severity.

text.text: It must also be considered that in some individuals anticipatory avoidance may function to limit exposure to triggering sounds, potentially contributing to the lower symptom severity observed in this profile.
This raises the question of whether some degree of avoidance may be functional for certain individuals with misophonia by helping to alleviate symptom burden, which warrants future investigation.
Within the reactive-and anticipatory-dominant profiles, we observed intriguing negative correlations between anticipatory and reactive avoidance.
This suggests that individuals within these subgroups tend to rely predominantly on one specific strategy over the other.

Importantly, because these behaviors were assessed in two independent measurement conditions, this negative relationship is not a methodological dependency, such as the impossibility of escaping from a sound that had already been prevented.
This pattern may have several clinically meaningful explanations.
For individuals with an anticipatory-dominant profile, strong reliance on preventing exposure may reduce opportunities to develop and practice coping strategies during actual trigger exposure.
When exposure nevertheless occurs, either by choice or unavoidably, these individuals may therefore tend to show relatively little reactive escape.
One possibility is that they consciously mobilize their resources to endure aversive stimuli.
It could be related to internalized beliefs (e.g., "I should not react like this."), or a self-perception of high coping competence (e.g., "I can handle this without leaving.").
It could also be driven by motivational factors, such as social desirability or test motivation (e.g., a desire to comply with the experimenter's instructions).

Alternatively, their habitual reliance on preventing exposure may leave them with limited effective situational coping strategies (e.g., putting on headphones or leaving the room) once the trigger has occurred.

Consequently, instead of engaging in reactive escape (a 'flight' response), they may remain in the situation despite considerable distress, potentially resembling a freezing or behavioral inhibition response.
However, freezing behavior is conceptually distinct from both anticipatory and reactive avoidance and was not separately assessed in the present study.
Conversely, individuals with a reactive-dominant profile may not anticipate trigger situations as sufficiently aversive or uncontrollable to justify a preventive response.
Instead, avoidance may become behaviorally relevant only once the trigger is actually present and the aversive response exceeds a situational threshold.

Repeated experiences in which terminating exposure produces rapid relief could further reinforce escape through negative reinforcement, making reactive avoidance an increasingly dominant coping response.
Thus, these individuals may enter potentially triggering situations relatively readily but rely on escape once distress becomes acute.
Over time, this pattern could restrict opportunities to develop coping strategies that allow continued engagement with the situation despite ongoing trigger exposure.
The negative association between anticipatory and reactive avoidance may therefore reflect different learned regulatory behaviors.
Both patterns could limit the development of flexible situational coping.

While in the high affective and anticipatory profiles the severity of aversive reactions to sounds was associated with at least one form of avoidance, in the reactive-dominant reactivity profile, avoidance behaviors and sound aversion were not correlated.
One possibility for this decoupling is that once a trigger occurs, individuals in this group tend to escape or disengage regardless of whether the sound is moderately or extremely aversive.
In this case, the urge to escape may be governed more by an automatic behavioral response than by the situational intensity of the emotional reaction itself.
A second possibility is that reactive-dominant individuals simply have a wider threshold for tolerating sounds.

Another possibility is that this avoidance reaction could be triggered by a rapid, intense physiological response, such as muscle tension, rather than by a conscious cognitive assessment of the emotion during exposure.

The critical role of immediate physiological arousal is well supported in recent literature. Andermane et al. (2023) identified body tension as the most important distinguishing feature of the misophonic response profile.
text.formatted: The critical role of immediate physiological arousal is well supported in recent literature. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Andermane et al. (2023)</ref> identified body tension as the most important distinguishing feature of the misophonic response profile.

text.text: Similarly, Woolley et al. (2025) observed that individuals across distinct subgroups exhibit pronounced physiological reactions during actual exposure to trigger sounds.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al. (2025)</ref> observed that individuals across distinct subgroups exhibit pronounced physiological reactions during actual exposure to trigger sounds.

text.text: Thus, reactive-dominant individuals may also be fleeing from the immediate physical discomfort rather than the cognitive appraisal of the sound's aversiveness.
A particularly noteworthy finding of this study is the limited convergence between the behavioral and self-report measures.
Most strikingly, the consistent absence of a distinct reactive subgroup in self-report measures raises important questions about the inherent limitations of retrospective assessment.
It may suggest that standard questionnaires capture more average dispositional behavior, whereas behavioral measures capture specific coping strategies employed in particular situations.

In previous studies, misophonia profiles were distinguished based primarily on self-report measures (e.g., Andermane et al., 2023; Norris et al., 2022) or clinician-administered interviews (Woolley et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In previous studies, misophonia profiles were distinguished based primarily on self-report measures (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Andermane et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Norris et al., 2022)</ref> or clinician-administered interviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Woolley et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present study builds upon this foundation by incorporating a standardized behavioral assessment.
While this behavioral test offers a more objective measure of situational reactivity, it inherently raises important questions regarding its ecological validity.
Misophonic triggers are often highly idiosyncratic, and individual reactions are deeply context-dependent (Humolli et al., 2026; Savard et al., 2022; Siepsiak et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Misophonic triggers are often highly idiosyncratic, and individual reactions are deeply context-dependent <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Humolli et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Savard et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Siepsiak et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the controlled environment of the M-BAT may not fully encapsulate the complexity of real-world misophonic encounters.
However, in this study, individuals were asked to indicate their level of idiosyncrasy, and we found no significant association with the behavioral measures.
Furthermore, retrospective self-reports are susceptible to memory and response biases, lack a clear frame of reference, and require some level of awareness of avoidance.
All of these aspects may have contributed to the differences observed between self-report and behavioral profiles.

Specifically, performance on the M-BAT may reflect a situational coping strategy (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984) employed by participants at a particular moment, rather than a stable dispositional style (Moos & Holahan, 2003).

text.text: Further studies could evaluate avoidance within the broader context of other coping strategies, as well as coping flexibility in employing a variety of strategies tailored to situational demands (Cheng et al., 2014) and their short-and long-term adaptiveness.

text.text: Self-reported reactive and anticipatory avoidance were highly correlated, which may partly explain why no qualitatively distinct self-reported subgroups emerged.
In addition, the relatively low reliability of some self-report measures may have reduced the ability to detect qualitatively distinct profiles by attenuating individual differences.
At the same time, the high correlation raises questions about the discriminant validity of the two BMQ-R avoidance scales.
Re-examining the wording of the items revealed some overlap in the temporal functions of the two avoidance behaviors, which may limit their discriminant validity.

Alternatively, individuals with misophonia may genuinely exhibit both forms of avoidance at similar levels or may not clearly distinguish between them, consistent with previous findings suggesting that individuals do not fully differentiate between situational distress and avoidance (Gámez et al., 2010).

text.text: Similarly, the construct validity of the M-BAT also qualifies the interpretation of the behavioral profiles. Remmert, Gregory, et al. (2026) showed that the behavioral indicators are partly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors (e.g., motivation) or do not fully differentiate between reactive and anticipatory avoidance.

(2026)</ref> showed that the behavioral indicators are partly influenced by construct-irrelevant factors (e.g., motivation) or do not fully differentiate between reactive and anticipatory avoidance.

text.text: Consequently, the identified profiles may not solely reflect distinct avoidance strategies.
Importantly, the modest correspondence between behavioral and self-report classifications suggests that these methods are not interchangeable.

Rather than viewing behavioral assessment merely as an alternative measurement approach, the present findings indicate that it may capture functionally relevant aspects of affective reactivity that are only incompletely represented in dispositional questionnaires.
The additional exploratory profile analysis, using both self-reported and behavioral indicators, revealed an interesting pattern that offers another perspective.

While one profile corresponded to the high affective reactivity profiles found in the other analyses, that is, above-average mean scores on all indicators, the other two profiles exhibited discrepancies in assessment modalities.
Specifically, anticipatory avoidance behavior was above average in one subgroup and below average in the other; however, self-reported anticipatory avoidance was almost identical in both profiles.
That means that either group under-or overestimates their observed avoidance behavior.
It may be interesting to investigate the group of individuals that show this discrepancy in future studies.

Possible explanations include that these individuals have limited awareness of their actual avoidance behavior, or that sound idiosyncrasy plays a more vital role and therefore situational behavioral responses in the standardized test differ from their own experiences.

Although misophonia might superficially appear to be a straightforward disorder, defined simply by intense negative reactions to specific sounds, our profiling data, consistent with recent literature (e.g., Andermane et al., 2023; Norris et al., 2022; Woolley et al., 2025), underscores its underlying complexity.
text.formatted: Although misophonia might superficially appear to be a straightforward disorder, defined simply by intense negative reactions to specific sounds, our profiling data, consistent with recent literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Andermane et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Norris et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Woolley et al., 2025)</ref>, underscores its underlying complexity.

text.text: These findings suggest that clinical assessment should not be limited to evaluating the severity of a simple stimulus-response reaction.
Instead, clinicians should conduct a careful behavioral analysis of the individual's specific response patterns as an initial step toward intervention planning.

This includes evaluating not only cognitive schemas and internalizing/externalizing beliefs (e.g., Remmert, Jebens et al., 2022; Vitoratou et al., 2021), but also the specific situational coping strategies employed (e.g., anticipatory versus reactive avoidance) and their functional utility.
text.formatted: This includes evaluating not only cognitive schemas and internalizing/externalizing beliefs (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Remmert, Jebens et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Vitoratou et al., 2021)</ref>, but also the specific situational coping strategies employed (e.g., anticipatory versus reactive avoidance) and their functional utility.

text.text: A process-based (e.g., Hofmann & Hayes, 2019) or a formulation-based approach (e.g., Gregory & Foster, 2023; Thrower et al., 2024) provides a more adequate framework for addressing the nuanced complexity of misophonic experiences, highlighting that 'one-size-fits-all' treatment protocols are likely insufficient.
text.formatted: A process-based (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Hofmann & Hayes, 2019)</ref> or a formulation-based approach (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Gregory & Foster, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Thrower et al., 2024)</ref> provides a more adequate framework for addressing the nuanced complexity of misophonic experiences, highlighting that 'one-size-fits-all' treatment protocols are likely insufficient.

text.text: In a recent qualitative study (Siepsiak et al., 2026), participants in a cognitive reappraisal session expressed the need for individualization of the intervention.
text.formatted: In a recent qualitative study <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Siepsiak et al., 2026)</ref>, participants in a cognitive reappraisal session expressed the need for individualization of the intervention.

text.text: For example, it was noted that not everybody experiences anticipatory anxiety before the trigger onset; therefore, clinicians should not overfocus on this phase, also during assessment.
Here, the behavioral data corroborate this clinical observation, demonstrating that individuals with misophonia differ significantly in their behavioral coping strategies.
For patients with a reactive-dominant profile, clinicians should not overemphasize anticipatory mechanisms.
Conversely, for those with an anticipatory-dominant profile, interventions targeting preemptive distress may be helpful, such as mindfulness, attentional training, or relaxation techniques.

The efficacy of such psychological interventions in misophonia has been preliminarily supported by recent randomized controlled trials for misophonia (see Lewin et al., 2026; Twohig et al., 2026) and could be particularly beneficial.
text.formatted: The efficacy of such psychological interventions in misophonia has been preliminarily supported by recent randomized controlled trials for misophonia (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Lewin et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Twohig et al., 2026)</ref> and could be particularly beneficial.

text.text: Ultimately, the natural variability in coping styles and the functional utility of specific strategies could be directly discussed with patients during therapy, as part of psychoeducation.

More broadly, these findings are consistent with a process-based perspective on psychopathology, in which clinically relevant heterogeneity is understood as differences in interacting regulatory processes.

From this perspective, the identified behavioral profiles may Importantly, we advocate extending diagnostic assessments beyond nominal categories to incorporate dimensional and functional profiles, with a specific focus on the utility of coping strategies.

Furthermore, given that misophonia is distinct from anxiety disorders (Rosenthal et al., 2026), clinicians should not assume avoidance to be a maladaptive strategy, especially since there is currently no robust evidence that avoidance serves as a maintenance factor in misophonia.
text.formatted: Furthermore, given that misophonia is distinct from anxiety disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Rosenthal et al., 2026)</ref>, clinicians should not assume avoidance to be a maladaptive strategy, especially since there is currently no robust evidence that avoidance serves as a maintenance factor in misophonia.

text.text: Instead of aiming for the complete elimination of avoidance, therapeutic efforts should foster coping flexibility (Cheng et al., 2014), equipping patients with the metaskills to flexibly adjust their coping strategies to specific situational demands (Moos & Holahan, 2003).
text.formatted: Instead of aiming for the complete elimination of avoidance, therapeutic efforts should foster coping flexibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Cheng et al., 2014)</ref>, equipping patients with the metaskills to flexibly adjust their coping strategies to specific situational demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Moos & Holahan, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: This study is not without limitations, which highlight important avenues for future research.

First, although the M-BAT adds a novel, more objective dimension to the assessment of actual misophonic behavior, overcoming several biases inherent in self-report, it may have limited ecological validity.

Since performing standardized behavioral tests in naturalistic settings remains challenging, future studies should focus on incorporating real-life context into measurement, such as using personalized triggers or Virtual Reality (VR) environments.

Second, based on the current data, we do not know whether the M-BAT captures a stable coping style (i.e., a pervasive dispositional trait) or rather a situational coping strategy employed at a specific moment.
To disentangle this question, future research should incorporate repeated-measures designs across various contexts (even if experimental).

Comparing behavioral performance with comprehensive clinical evaluations or real-time tracking methods (e.g., Ecological Momentary Assessment) could further clarify the stability and situational variability of these reactivity profiles.
Third, the assessment of reactive and anticipatory avoidance through self-report remains limited.
As the BMQ-R is currently the only instrument designed to distinguish between these two forms of avoidance, further psychometric evaluation, particularly of their discriminant validity, is needed.
Fourth, the sampling strategy limits the generalizability of the findings.
While the findings are expected to generalize to adults with subclinical or clinically relevant misophonic symptoms, the sample was self-selected, collected online, and mainly female.
Self-selection may have introduced bias, as individuals willing to participate in a behavioral assessment may differ systematically from those who chose not to participate.
For example, the sample may disproportionately include individuals with lower levels of avoidance behavior.
Finally, although the identified profiles proved theoretically meaningful and clinically interpretable, they should not be understood as evidence for natural categories of misophonia.
Thus, the identified profiles require replication across independent samples and assessment paradigms.

Taken together, the present findings suggest that heterogeneity in coping strategies for persons with misophonia may be better understood in terms of patterns of responding than differences in symptom severity alone.

Standardized behavioral assessment revealed qualitatively distinct and functionally meaningful reactivity profiles, whereas self-report measures primarily reflected gradations in overall affective reactivity, suggesting that the apparent latent structure of misophonia depends not only on the underlying phenomenon but also on how it is assessed.
By integrating behavioral assessment with self-report measures, the present study demonstrates the added value of directly assessing situational coping behavior.

Understanding individuals' patterns of anticipatory and reactive avoidance behavior may improve functional assessment, advance theoretical models of misophonia, and may contribute to more individualized interventions.

More broadly, these findings highlight the importance of complementing dispositional questionnaires with standardized behavioral assessment when investigating heterogeneity in psychopathology and suggest that future research should increasingly focus on behavioral patterns of responding across contexts to advance both the assessment and theoretical understanding of misophonia.
